description:
These two love-birds were seated overlooking my balconey and were a fantastic reference with the interesting colours reflected off their feathers. I also loved how the underlying yellow in their feathers was affected by the sunlight on them, diffusing through and creating an interesting warmth to what is normally a very cold white.

Cockatoos are fascinating, so smart and social but also so destructive at times. A tiny bit like humans.

The Original watercolour (still available) has slightly more detail and a darker background below the branch, please contact me if you wish to see it. Limited edition prints are the same as the shown image, 24/25 prints still available.

I was inspired by Annabel Armstrong's photographs of Rainbow Lorikeets that were posted on a free to use for artists site. The finished work is a combination of Annabel's references and my own and was an interesting challenge to balance the watercolour and ink drawing techniques together.

I love the pun of them enjoying the nectar of the Umbrella tree and have included a backdrop of the misty/rainy landscape that I often see looking out over the Lane Cove National Park. There are also two little honey bees foraging for nectar in the wet flowers.

The original and some limited edition prints are available.

This little Splendid Fairy Wren was created from a combination of sources and a large amount of imagination. The bug is loosely based on a flying termite but could be anything really. I thought it just needed to look tasty to a little wren looking for dinner. It started as a small study and then expanded to the whole page as I enjoyed it so much. I kept the colours simple with only a little accent blue on the wrens eye, with warm beak colours and some soft browns on the feathers.

The original was sold but limited edition prints are available.

This was a commissioned after a client saw my Mermaid painting at the Easter Show and discovered it had already been bought.

I created this version in a very similar way, with a pour of high flow acrylic paint and pouring medium for the water. I then painted into it to increase the realism.

The client offered to pose for the meremaid and I painted her into foreground once the water had dried, along with the rocks and shallow water. I used irridescent paint for her scales and hair, along with gold acrylic, which gave a pleasing shimmer in changing light.

This painting, part of a continuing Teatime Still Life series, captures a fleeting yet deeply personal moment, where light, colour, and ritual come together in quiet harmony. Set on a kitchen counter, the scene centres around the preparation of peppermint tea, with my favourite teapot rendered in luminous iridescent blues and purples. Around it sits a collection of rainbow-hued glasses, each one tied to a member of my family, an everyday arrangement that for me is both intimate and symbolic.

hat I feel elevated the whole still life was in fact the morning light. Streaming through the glassware, it refracted into a spectrum of colour that danced across the surface and turned a simple every day setting into a celebration of vibrancy and life. I chose to capture the scene midway through the act of making tea as it was too beautiful to not paint. I think this preserved the authenticity of the moment, although I had to remake the tea. It got cold as I was taking reference photo’s.

The painting carries a deeper meaning as well, serving as a tribute to rainbows, neurodiversity, and the full spectrum of human expression. The varied colours of the glasses become more than aesthetic as they suggest individuality within unity, difference held together in a shared, welcoming space.

I also love the ritual of tea making, the quiet contemplative feeling of filling a kettle with boiling water, the rising steam, the smell of tea-leaves and the warmth that comes with sharing it with others.

A rainbow lorikeet appears at the window, peering inside. Bathed in the brilliance of the outdoor light, it contrasts with the softer, more sheltered interior. Its presence suggests curiosity and connection, a bridge between the outside world and the sanctuary within. The kitchen becomes a place of refuge, warmth, and colour, quietly inviting both people and creatures to share in its calm.

Altogether, the painting is a celebration of light, ritual, and belonging, where the ordinary becomes radiant, and the preparation of tea transforms into an expression of comfort, inclusivity, and home.

In this drawing I wanted to capture a raw, untamed moment of intensity. The horses are locked in combat, their bodies coiled with energy and emotion. Rather than the familiar image of calm, docile farm animals, these horses are fierce and unrestrained, with bared teeth and wild eyes revealing a side of their nature that is powerful, unpredictable, and deeply primal.

The composition is driven by movement and tension. Muscles strain, heads arch, and forms collide, conveying both conflict and vitality. The energy is immediate and visceral, drawing the viewer into the clash. One horse is seeking dominance over the other, but the disadvantaged horse is not ready to submit.

I was initially inspired by a wonderful photo by Susie Bell of wild Salt River horses. I’ve replaced the original cool natural bush tones with a fiery sunset backdrop, an environment that feels less like a physical place and more like an embodiment of the horses’ spirit. Starting with a watercolour wash as a sort of base to work over, I drew over it all with a range of fine tip colour pens. Reds, oranges, and yellows dominate the scene, radiating heat and intensity. I was going to add more red to the actual horses but I really liked the intensity of the white paper against the red background and instead worked it slowly up with many light layers of lines, using both cross hatching and form lines. The drawing process worked its own magic, and I ended up with an image I had not planned but definitely preferred. Against the background, the two fighting horses’ white dappled coats make them appear almost incandescent, as if their inner ferocity is manifesting outward. Their whiteness is not soft, but heat at its most extreme, a white-hot flame that suggests both power and purity of instinct.

There is also a deeper cultural and symbolic layer within the work. Drawing from an Australian perspective, to me the Salt River horses echo the spirit of the Brumbies, wild, independent, and fiercely self-determined. This connection reinforces the theme of freedom and resistance, of creatures that cannot be easily tamed.

Created in recognition of the Year of the Fire Horse, the drawing becomes more than a study of motion and form—it is a tribute to a particular kind of energy: bold, passionate, and unstoppable.

This oil painting invites the viewer into a quiet moment where fantasy and the everyday gently intertwine. At its heart, a Halfling (or Hobbit) sits just outside her hidden burrow, absorbed in the simple wonder of a pale moth flitting above her hands, in the glow of her lantern. I intended a scene that was tranquil and grounded, yet quietly enchanted, a world where magic exists not as spectacle, but as something familiar.

Inspired by LoTR and tabletop role-playing worlds, the piece leans away from grand, heroic imagery and instead celebrates a more humble kind of magic. The palette plays a central role in establishing this mood. Rich greens and Burnt Sienna dominate the background, evoking the textures of leaves and tree bark. The lighting suggests early evening. Teal twilight colours in the distance and warm creamy light in the foreground from the lantern, evoking a gentle, diffused glow that enhances the sense of quiet magic.

The background is kept loose and impressionistic, allowing the environment to feel alive and atmospheric. In contrast, the Halfling is painted with greater detail, drawing the viewer’s eye in towards her hands and face and anchoring the composition emotionally. Although the moth is imaginary, it is based on a hawk moth. It becomes both a focal point and a small, luminous bridge between the natural and the magical. Its presence feels playful and personal, hinting at a deeper story just beyond the frame. It is also a nod to the model Nicole’s love of insects and in particular moths. Her online information posts on insects are wonderful.

My source material for this painting were reference photographs provided by the painter and illustrator Howard Lyon (of Nicole), for the character and lighting. I also used some personal photos of the forest walks in the park below my home for the background and colours.

medium: Ink pen, acrylic pen and watercolour pencils.

description: This was a surprisingly fast painting, it took less than a week, despite the detail and size. I was experimenting with a looser style and had to limit myself. I love the expression on the Dragon's face in the foreground - debating whether the bee is edible or a bad idea! A wiser - perhaps more experienced Water Dragon looks on from the background, watching to see what will happen. I added the bee halfway through the painting and loved how suddenly there was a story, just because of how the Dragon needed a reason to be looking up with such curiosity. Sometimes the painting is kind enough to show you what it wants as you are working on it.
